evaluation.positioning_hook: A young lifeguard trapped overnight in a locked aquatic center must survive two vengeful survivors, a weaponized boyfriend, and a viral humiliation plot before the deep water turns into her execution chamber.

audience_appeal_marketability.reasoning: The premise is instantly legible and genre-forward: a contained survival nightmare with a female lead, a boyfriend betrayal, and a viral-shame engine. It has a clear audience in elevated genre buyers and streamer horror-thriller fans, though the specific aquatic-center setting and mean-spirited turn make it narrower than a broad four-quadrant play.

conceptual_hook_clarity.reasoning: The hook lands early and cleanly: Michelle rescues Raven, then gets trapped with her in the same aquatic center as the night turns predatory. The diving well, the locked building, and the rescue-turned-revenge premise are easy to pitch in two sentences.

character_appeal_and_long_term_potential.reasoning: Michelle has a strong physical and emotional profile — capable, anxious, and increasingly cornered — and Raven is a vivid antagonist with real volatility. Daniel and Angelo add useful pressure, though they function more as engines of betrayal than as deeply layered people.

creative_originality_and_boldness.reasoning: The script takes a familiar trapped-thriller setup and gives it a fresh arena in the aquatic center, with the diving well and water-based geography doing real story work. The AI-altered humiliation video and the rescue-backlash idea are contemporary and sharp, even if the overall revenge-thriller spine is recognizable.

narrative_momentum_engagement.reasoning: Once the lights go out, the script keeps escalating through theft, betrayal, bodily threat, chemical attack, and underwater survival. The set pieces are clearly staged and the pressure keeps tightening, especially from the locker-room reveal through the chlorine-gas sequence and final dive.

resonant_originality.reasoning: The core idea feels fresh because the central contradiction is immediate and memorable: saving people makes Michelle a target. The child-sized skull, the viral video, and the aquatic-center geography give the premise a distinct identity, even though the revenge-thriller mechanics themselves are familiar.

world_density_and_texture.reasoning: The aquatic center is more than a backdrop; the pool deck, diving well, observation window, service corridor, surge tank, and mechanical room all create usable geography. The world feels operational and specific, with liability, rescue protocols, and maintenance infrastructure feeding the plot.

tonal_specificity.reasoning: The script has a crisp blend of erotic tension, survival horror, and darkly comic menace, especially in the banter between Michelle and Raven and Daniel’s increasingly twisted lines. The tone is distinctive enough to stand out, though it occasionally shifts from flirtation to brutality very quickly.

latent_depth_slow_burn_potential.reasoning: There are seeds of a bigger idea about rescue, public humiliation, and the cost of being seen as a hero, but the script mostly externalizes that through plot pressure. The child skull and the news-broadcast epilogue hint at a larger mythology, though the feature largely plays as a contained nightmare.

relationship_density_and_ensemble_engine.reasoning: Michelle/Raven is the engine, with Daniel and Angelo providing strong pressure points, but the relationship web is not especially expansive beyond those three. The script gets a lot of mileage from the triangle and the betrayal reveals, yet it remains fundamentally a lead-driven feature rather than an ensemble machine.

lead_characters.name: Michelle
lead_characters.demographics: Woman, early 20s, lifeguard with Coast Guard ambitions; physically capable, emotionally guarded, likely white/ambiguous from page.
lead_characters.hook: Michelle is a disciplined young lifeguard who wants to turn competence into a future, but her need to be seen as heroic becomes the very thing that traps her. She starts as controlled and self-conscious, then gets forced into a brutal test of nerve in the one environment she knows best, where her fear of deep water becomes psychological as much as physical.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of a rising genre lead like Maika Monroe in The Guest or Willa Fitzgerald in Scream — a role that lets an actor play vulnerability, physical command, panic, and hard-earned defiance in one contained pressure cooker.

lead_characters.name: Raven
lead_characters.demographics: Woman, early 20s, affluent or protected by family, non-swimmer, sexually fluid or coded as queer, volatile and image-conscious.
lead_characters.hook: Raven enters as the rescued victim and quickly reveals herself as a resentful, manipulative, and deeply wounded force who weaponizes humiliation as self-defense. She’s seductive, funny, and unstable, with a sharp instinct for control that makes her feel like both victim and predator.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gives an actor the same volatile showcase as Jena Malone in The Neon Demon or Rebecca Hall in Resurrection — a character who can pivot from wounded intimacy to outright menace without losing magnetism.

lead_characters.name: Daniel
lead_characters.demographics: Man, 20s, Michelle’s boyfriend, hospital-scrubs surgeon-in-training, handsome, emotionally insecure.
lead_characters.hook: Daniel starts as supportive comic relief and gradually curdles into the most intimate betrayal in the script, revealing a brittle ego underneath the charm. His turn is personal, petty, and ugly, which makes him more dangerous than a standard boyfriend antagonist.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is strong supporting-antagonist material in the vein of Penn Badgley’s early You or Nicholas Hoult in The Menu — a role that lets an actor play charm, wounded vanity, and a sudden, ugly moral collapse.

lead_characters.name: Angelo
lead_characters.demographics: Man, 20s, Italian-coded charmer, janitor at the aquatic center, football-scholarship dreamer.
lead_characters.hook: Angelo is the flirtatious, socially agile outsider who turns out to be carrying his own humiliation and rage, then channels it into sadistic payback. He’s the script’s most overtly theatrical antagonist, equal parts wounded ego and physical threat.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gives an actor a scene-stealing villain turn like Jack Huston in Fargo or Ben Barnes in The Punisher — charisma first, then a hard pivot into menace and physical danger.

lead_characters.name: Karla
lead_characters.hook: Karla is the pragmatic adult in the room, the one person consistently thinking about liability, staffing, and the real-world consequences of Michelle’s choices. She grounds the script’s world and gives the facility a believable institutional voice.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of grounded authority role that lets an actor do the efficient, lived-in work of a Colman Domingo in support mode or a Patricia Clarkson-style manager figure — calm, specific, and quietly memorable.

lead_characters.name: Kris
lead_characters.hook: Kris arrives late as a practical rescuer and becomes the final note of ambiguity, because Michelle’s trauma has made even help feel suspect. He’s not a major engine, but he gives the ending a chilling aftertaste.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is compact, efficient character-actor material — the kind of role that gives an actor a clean, credible button like a Michael Stuhlbarg or Shea Whigham scene, where a few minutes can land hard.

casting_characteristics: One lead with strong physicality and emotional range
Two supporting male antagonists with distinct charisma profiles
One supporting female antagonist with sexualized volatility
No child performers required despite child-skull prop

notable_requirements: Aquatic center with pool deck, diving well, locker room, lobby, office, service corridor, mechanical room, surge tank room
Night shoot coverage for the bulk of the thriller action
Water-safe production design and wet-set continuity

technical.vfx_details: Primarily practical with limited digital cleanup for the AI-altered video, blood/water continuity, and any safety-assisted diving or underwater inserts.
technical.sfx_needs: Chlorine-gas effect, broken plaque/shiv prop, gunshot impact, underwater struggle, emergency lighting failure, practical water effects, blood and chemical burn makeup.

rights_flags.detail: TikTok-style viral video language and social-platform references are present but not central enough to require a specific platform clearance.

platform_fit.series_engine_or_release_model: Feature release model: contained streamer thriller with festival-to-platform or direct-streaming potential.

budget.note: The aquatic-center build, wet-set continuity, night work, underwater action, chlorine-gas sequence, and emergency-lighting blackout all push this above a simple contained interior thriller.

casting.note: Michelle needs a lead who can carry physical action, erotic tension, panic, and final-girl resolve; Raven, Daniel, and Angelo each need a distinct tonal register so the betrayals land cleanly.

development.note: The premise is clear, but the script is built on a strong tonal balance between flirtation, humiliation, and horror; that balance is the main thing buyers will test in the room.

comp_set.title: The Invitation
comp_set.why_it_comps: Like this script, it turns a contained social setup into a slow-burn trap where trust curdles into threat.

comp_set.title: The Black Phone
comp_set.why_it_comps: It shares the same premium-genre lane of a young protagonist under escalating, claustrophobic threat with strong atmospheric control.

comp_set.title: Fresh
comp_set.why_it_comps: The script has the same mix of flirtation, bodily danger, and darkly comic menace that makes a relationship-driven thriller feel current.

comp_set.title: Barbarian
comp_set.why_it_comps: It uses a single location with hidden layers and escalating reversals to keep the audience off balance.

audience_target.primary_audience: Adults who like elevated, female-led survival thrillers with a nasty romantic edge and a strong contained-location hook.
audience_target.demographics: 18-44 skew, slightly female-leaning, streamer-native genre audience, strong appeal to horror/thriller fans and date-night viewers who tolerate mature content.

budget_tier.note: A single primary location, limited cast, and mostly practical effects keep it in indie feature territory, with cost pressure coming from the aquatic-center build and night water work.

types_of_buyers: indie distributors looking for a female-led hook
lane_fit.detail: This sits naturally in the lane where a sharp premise, a strong lead role, and a manageable location footprint can sell the movie before the cast is fully locked. The aquatic-center setting gives it a visual identity that feels more specific than a generic home-invasion or cabin thriller.

ip_potential.detail: Standalone feature. The child-skull tease suggests mythology, but there is no clear franchise vector or spin-off character with independent depth on the page.

strengths.what_it_means: This gives the movie a built-in production moat: one location can deliver multiple distinct set pieces without feeling repetitive. Buyers like contained thrillers that still feel visually engineered, and this one has a clear spatial identity.
strengths.evidence: Pool deck, diving well, locker room, observation window, service corridor, surge tank, and mechanical room all become active parts of the chase.

strengths.dimension_or_area: Michelle is a clean genre lead.
strengths.what_it_means: The role can sell on casting because it offers physical competence, sexual tension, fear, and a final moral pivot. That combination is exactly what makes a mid-budget thriller feel premium rather than disposable.
strengths.evidence: Her fear of deep water, her Coast Guard ambition, and her eventual turn from panic to tactical defiance on the diving board.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The rescue-backlash premise is instantly ownable.
strengths.what_it_means: The movie has a sharp commercial engine: the people Michelle saves become the people who destroy her. That’s a clean hook for marketing and a strong reason for audiences to lean in beyond the basic trapped-thriller setup.
strengths.evidence: Angelo and Raven explicitly blame Michelle for how their lives changed after the rescue, and Daniel’s betrayal extends the same idea into the intimate sphere.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The set pieces escalate with real variety.
strengths.what_it_means: The script doesn’t rely on one repeated scare pattern; it moves from flirtation to blackout to chemical attack to underwater survival. That makes the movie easier to sell as an event thriller rather than a single-note chamber piece.
strengths.evidence: Locker-room steam sequence, chlorine-drum attack, surge-tank chase, underwater dive, and final gunfight in the well.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The tone has a nasty, current edge.
strengths.what_it_means: The mix of sexual charge, humiliation culture, and bodily threat feels contemporary and market-aware. That makes it attractive to buyers looking for genre material that can travel on vibe as much as plot.
strengths.evidence: The AI-altered humiliation video, Raven’s social-media obsession, and the script’s darkly comic sexual banter.

whats_special.headline: This is a contained, female-led thriller with a sharp commercial engine and a location that does real work. The aquatic-center setting, the rescue-backlash premise, and the escalating practical set pieces make it feel like a streamer-ready genre buy that can be sold on concept before cast attachment.

items.area: The tonal pivot from flirtation to torture is abrupt.
items.detail: The script moves from playful chemistry in the pool and locker room to coercion, chemical assault, and gun violence very quickly. That can play as bold, but it also narrows the margin for buyers who want the erotic-thriller energy without the harder horror turn.

items.area: Daniel’s turn needs a very specific actor.
items.detail: He goes from supportive boyfriend to bitter, chemically sadistic antagonist, and the script asks the audience to accept that pivot in a short span. That role will live or die on casting because the emotional betrayal has to feel personal, not just plot-convenient.

items.area: The aquatic-center build is not free.
items.detail: The pool deck, diving well, locker room, service corridor, surge tank, and mechanical room all need to feel distinct and playable, and the night-water continuity is doing a lot of heavy lifting. This is still an indie feature, but it is not a cheap one.

items.area: The ending teases a larger mythology without fully paying it off.
items.detail: The child-sized skull, the news montage, and the implication that saved people may become attackers point toward a broader horror engine, but the feature itself stays mostly contained. Buyers will notice that tension between standalone thriller and franchise tease.

issues.headline: The script’s biggest friction is tonal: it wants to start as a charged, intimate thriller and then hard-shift into full survival horror, which will be a taste issue for some buyers. The other real conversations are casting Daniel correctly and deciding whether the aquatic-center scope stays comfortably inside indie economics.
